title: Thread-Safe Bounded Blocking Queue
description: Implement a bounded blocking queue from scratch using locks and condition variables. Producers block when full, consumers block when empty. The canonical concurrency primitive — if you can't implement this, you can't implement anything concurrent.
prompt: Implement a thread-safe bounded blocking queue with `put()` and `take()` methods. Producers block when the queue is full; consumers block when it's empty.
prompt_note: This is a **from-scratch implementation** problem — `java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue` already exists, but the interviewer wants to see you wire up the locks and conditions yourself. The design is small but every line matters. Getting the `await`/`signal` semantics right is the entire point.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Should this be a generic queue — `BoundedBlockingQueue<T>` — or fixed to a type?"
You: "Should `put()` and `take()` block indefinitely, or support timeouts?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Both versions. `put(x)` blocks forever; `offer(x, timeout)` returns false if timeout expires."
clarifying_questions.why: Two API variants. The timed version uses `Condition.awaitNanos()` with loop for spurious wakeups.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "FIFO ordering guaranteed?"
clarifying_questions.why: Use an `ArrayDeque` or circular array — both give O(1) FIFO operations.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "What's the use case — producer-consumer pattern?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes. Multiple producers and consumers running concurrently."
clarifying_questions.why: Must handle **many-producers/many-consumers**, not just 1:1. This affects notification strategy (`signal` vs `signalAll`).

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Can the queue be closed? What happens to blocked threads if it is?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes — support `close()`. Blocked consumers should be woken up and see an empty+closed queue (throw or return null)."
clarifying_questions.why: Graceful shutdown is a common follow-up. Add a `closed` flag + wake all waiters.

core: `put(item)` — add to the back of the queue. **Blocks** if full until space available.
`take()` — remove from the front. **Blocks** if empty until an item is available.
`offer(item, timeout)` — like `put` but returns `false` if timeout expires.
`poll(timeout)` — like `take` but returns `null` if timeout expires.
`close()` — graceful shutdown. Wake all waiters. Further `put` throws; `take` returns remaining items then throws.
out_of_scope: Priority ordering, persistence, distributed coordination, fair ordering between producers/consumers.

core: **Strict FIFO** — items come out in insertion order.
**No busy-waiting** — threads must block via condition variables, not spin.
**No lost wakeups** — every `put` that adds an item must ensure at least one blocked consumer is woken.
**Handle spurious wakeups** — `await()` must be in a `while` loop, not `if`.
out_of_scope: Fairness guarantees (e.g., longest-waiting producer first), lock-free implementations.

primary_scope: `put(x)` → acquire lock → while full: await notFull → add → signal notEmpty → unlock
`take()` → acquire lock → while empty: await notEmpty → remove → signal notFull → unlock
Timed variants use `awaitNanos()` with deadline tracking
`close()` sets flag and signals all conditions → waiters re-check and return/throw
termination_points: `NullPointerException` — null item in `put` (ArrayDeque disallows nulls by convention)
Timed variants: return `false` / `null` on timeout (not an exception)
entity_intro: This problem has exactly **one class**. Over-engineering with multiple entities is a red flag — the interviewer wants to see correct primitives, not architecture.

entities.name: BoundedBlockingQueue<T>
entities.role: **The entire problem.** Holds items, capacity, a `ReentrantLock`, two `Condition` objects (`notFull`, `notEmpty`), and a `closed` flag. All methods acquire the lock, wait on the appropriate condition, and signal the other condition after modification.

entities.name: Item wrapper
entities.role: Don't wrap items in a node class unless you need linking. `ArrayDeque<T>` already handles storage. No Item entity needed.

relationships.owns: `ArrayDeque<T>` storage, `ReentrantLock`, two `Condition` vars, capacity, closed flag

mvc_note: **MVC doesn't apply here** — this is a single-class concurrency primitive, not an application. The design principle is: **one lock + two conditions** — the Monitor Pattern from Hoare/Brinch-Hansen's 1970s papers. Don't invent extra layers.

code_sections.label: Core — Lock + Two Conditions
code_sections.flow: **One lock, two conditions.** `notFull` = producers wait here when queue is full. `notEmpty` = consumers wait here when queue is empty. `put()` waits on `notFull`, signals `notEmpty`. `take()` waits on `notEmpty`, signals `notFull`. This is the canonical bounded buffer solution.
code_sections.edge_cases: **Always use `while` not `if`** for wait loops — spurious wakeups are real. **Always signal the other condition** in a finally-like way — if you forget, the counterpart thread blocks forever.

code_sections.label: Timed Variants — offer() and poll() with Deadline
code_sections.flow: Use `Condition.awaitNanos(nanos)` instead of `await()`. It returns remaining nanos — use this to track remaining time across loop iterations (spurious wakeups can eat time).
code_sections.edge_cases: **Remaining nanos ≤ 0** → timeout expired, return false/null. **Interrupt** during await → `InterruptedException` is thrown, propagate it.

code_sections.label: Graceful Shutdown — close() with signalAll
code_sections.flow: Set `closed = true` → **`signalAll`** on both conditions to wake every blocked thread. Each awoken thread re-checks the loop condition and sees `closed` → throws or returns accordingly.
code_sections.edge_cases: **Must use `signalAll`, not `signal`** — multiple threads might be blocked on each condition. Waking only one leaves the others hanging forever.

patterns.name: Monitor Pattern (one lock + conditions)
patterns.why: Classical concurrency pattern: an object owns its state and a single lock that all methods acquire. Condition variables let threads wait inside the monitor for state changes. The canonical formulation of bounded-buffer by Hoare/Brinch-Hansen uses **exactly this structure**: one lock, two conditions — one per 'waiting for' predicate.
patterns.where: `ReentrantLock lock` + `notFull`, `notEmpty` conditions — one per wait predicate

patterns.name: Producer-Consumer
patterns.why: This queue **is** the decoupling primitive for the Producer-Consumer pattern. Producers don't need to know about consumers or vice versa — they only interact through the queue. The queue handles backpressure (blocking producers when full) and flow control (blocking consumers when empty).
patterns.where: The queue itself — no code to point to, it's the architectural role

concurrency.issue: Spurious wakeups — `await()` returns without being signaled
concurrency.fix: **Always use `while` not `if`** in the wait loop. JVM-level condition variables can return spuriously (rare, but specified by POSIX and Java docs). `while (queue.size() == capacity) await();` re-checks the condition on wakeup — if spurious, loops back to await. `if` would incorrectly proceed.

concurrency.issue: Lost wakeup — producer adds item but no consumer sees it
concurrency.fix: `await()` **atomically releases the lock and waits**. The producer can't acquire the lock and signal until the consumer has called `await()`. There's no window for the signal to be lost because the wait+release is atomic. **This is why you must wait while holding the lock — don't check the condition outside the lock.**

concurrency.issue: Thundering herd — `signalAll` wakes everyone, they all try to proceed
concurrency.fix: Use `signal` (wake one) for `put`/`take` — only one waiter can make progress at a time (there's only one new slot / one new item). `signalAll` is only for `close()` where every waiter needs to see the closed flag. **Wake exactly as many as can succeed** — wasteful wake-ups cause cache thrashing and lock contention.

`lockInterruptibly()` + `await()` both throw `InterruptedException`. The thread's interrupt flag is cleared when the exception is thrown. Propagate the exception (`throws InterruptedException`) so the caller can handle it. Don't swallow it — it's the **interruption contract** for blocking methods.

deep_dives.question: Why one lock and two conditions instead of two locks?
deep_dives.answer: Two locks (one for producers, one for consumers) would require coordinating state visibility between them — the `size` field would need to be atomic or cross-lock synchronized. **One lock with two conditions** is simpler and correct: all mutations happen under the same lock, so state is always consistent. The two conditions just let you wake producers and consumers independently. `LinkedBlockingQueue` actually uses two locks (`putLock`, `takeLock`) for throughput, but it's more complex and only wins under extreme contention.

deep_dives.question: Why `signal()` not `signalAll()` in put/take?
deep_dives.answer: Only one thread can benefit from a single new slot or item. `signalAll` wakes everyone; they all race to grab the lock, one wins, the rest go back to waiting. That's O(N) wasted wakeups. `signal` wakes exactly one — the other waiters stay blocked efficiently. **Exception:** `close()` needs `signalAll` because every waiter must re-check the `closed` flag.

deep_dives.question: Why `while` loop around `await()` instead of `if`?
deep_dives.answer: Three reasons: (1) **Spurious wakeups** — specified as possible by Java's Condition docs. (2) **Signal-based wakeups are stale** — another thread could acquire the lock between your wakeup and your re-check, changing state. (3) **Correctness** — re-checking is cheap, incorrect state progression is catastrophic. The rule: **wait in a while loop around the predicate, always.**

deep_dives.question: How does this compare to `java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue`?
deep_dives.answer: `ArrayBlockingQueue` uses the **exact same design**: one `ReentrantLock`, two `Condition` vars (`notEmpty`, `notFull`), circular array storage. You can literally look at its source — it's ~300 lines. Our implementation is simpler (ArrayDeque vs circular array) but semantically equivalent. `LinkedBlockingQueue` uses **two locks** for higher throughput but has weaker size consistency.

deep_dives.question: What's the deal with `lockInterruptibly()` vs `lock()`?
deep_dives.answer: `lock()` is **not** interruptible — if a thread is waiting for the lock and gets interrupted, it sets the interrupt flag but keeps waiting. `lockInterruptibly()` throws `InterruptedException` immediately on interrupt, even while waiting for the lock. For a blocking queue, interruption should propagate through **every** blocking point: waiting for the lock AND waiting on the condition. So always use `lockInterruptibly()` in blocking primitives.

deep_dives.question: How would you make this fair (longest-waiting thread goes first)?
deep_dives.answer: Use `new ReentrantLock(true)` — the `true` enables fair mode. Threads acquire the lock in FIFO order. **But** fair locks are ~10x slower than unfair ones due to the cost of maintaining the wait queue. Production code almost always uses unfair locks. Mention fairness exists; don't recommend it by default.

deep_dives.question: How would you make it lock-free?
deep_dives.answer: Use `ConcurrentLinkedQueue` (already unbounded lock-free, Michael-Scott algorithm). For bounded+lock-free: the **Disruptor** pattern (LMAX) uses a ring buffer with memory barriers and sequence counters — no locks, but complex. For an interview, mention that lock-free is possible but justify why locks are fine: contention on a single lock at O(1) per op is fast; the JVM handles bias-locking and escalation. Don't go lock-free unless profiling demands it.
